Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. A subset of
$X \times Y$ is a **measurable rectangle** if it has the form $A \times B$ with
$A \in \mathcal A$ and $B \in \mathcal B$.

The ambient sigma-algebras matter: the same set may be a measurable rectangle
for one pair $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)$ and not for another.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

derivations.claim: By induction on $n$, the finite product sigma-algebra is generated by the $n$-coordinate rectangles. The base case is $n=1$. At the induction step, let $\mathcal S$ be the sigma-algebra generated by $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangles. For each measurable last-coordinate set $B$, the class of first-coordinate sets $A$ with $A\times B\in\mathcal S$ is a sigma-algebra: it contains the whole first product since the whole-first-product times $B$ is a coordinate rectangle, and complements and countable unions follow by relative difference inside that set and by countable unions. It contains the $n$-coordinate rectangles by construction, so it contains the recursively defined $n$-fold product sigma-algebra. Thus $\mathcal S$ contains every rectangle used in the recursive binary product. Conversely, each $(n+1)$-coordinate rectangle belongs to that recursive product sigma-algebra by its defining binary rectangle clause, so the two generated sigma-algebras agree.

For a generating rectangle $E_1\times\cdots\times E_n$, its preimage under $f$ is $\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}(E_i)$. Each set in this finite intersection belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [A1], so the preimage belongs to $\mathcal F$ by [F4]. The class of target sets whose preimages under $f$ lie in $\mathcal F$ is a sigma-algebra because preimages preserve complements and countable unions; by step 1.1 it contains the generators, so it contains the product sigma-algebra and [F3] makes $f$ measurable.

For $\pi$ a permutation, $\tau_\pi^{-1}(E_1\times\cdots\times E_n)=E_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\times\cdots\times E_{\pi^{-1}(n)}$, which is a generating rectangle by [F2]. The same generated-sigma-algebra argument of step 2.1 proves that $\tau_\pi$ is measurable.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(S_i,\Sigma_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be finitely many measurable spaces, with
$n\ge1$, and equip $\prod_{i=1}^nS_i$ with its finite product sigma-algebra.
If $f_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ are measurable, then the tuple
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$ is measurable. If all factors equal one measurable space
$(S,\Sigma)$, every coordinate permutation $\tau_\pi:S^n\to S^n$ is
measurable, where $(\tau_\pi z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. If
$E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, then $E_x \in \mathcal B$ for every
$x \in X$ and $E^y \in \mathcal A$ for every $y \in Y$.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal D$ consist of product-measurable sets $E\subseteq\Omega\times S$ for which $k_E(\omega):=K(\omega,E_\omega)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $\int_H k_E\,dP=P(H\cap\{(\omega,X(\omega))\in E\})$ for every $H\in\mathcal G$. For a rectangle $E=A\times B$, $k_E=\mathbf1_AK(\cdot,B)$ is measurable by [F1], and its integral identity follows by applying [F1] to $H\cap A$. Thus all rectangles lie in $\mathcal D$.

For each $\omega$, define $\bar K(\omega,\cdot)=K(\omega,\cdot)\otimes\lambda$, which is a probability measure by [F4]. On a rectangle $B\times C$, its evaluation is $K(\omega,B)\lambda(C)$, a $\mathcal G$-measurable function. For $H\in\mathcal G$, the integral of this evaluation over $H$ equals $\lambda(C)P(H\cap\{X\in B\})$ by [F1]. Since $H\cap\{X\in B\}\in\mathcal G\vee\sigma(X)$, independence [A2, F5] makes this $P(H\cap\{X\in B\}\cap\{U\in C\})$.

The whole space is in $\mathcal D$. If $E\in\mathcal D$, then $k_{E^c}=1-k_E$ and the integral identity for $E^c$ follows by subtracting the identity for $E$ from $P(H)$. If $E_j$ are disjoint members of $\mathcal D$, then their sections are disjoint, so $k_{\cup_jE_j}=\sum_j k_{E_j}$ pointwise; [F8] makes the increasing partial sums' limit measurable, and [F6] gives the integral identity for the union. Hence $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. Measurable rectangles contain $\Omega\times S$ and are closed under finite intersections, so they form a pi-system generating $\mathcal G\otimes\Sigma$ by [F2]; [F7] therefore gives $\mathcal D=\mathcal G\otimes\Sigma$.

For $B\in\Tau$, [A1] makes $E=g^{-1}(B)$ product-measurable and [F10] makes its sections measurable, so $K_g(\omega,B)$ is defined. The map $\omega\mapsto(\omega,X(\omega))$ is measurable from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $(\Omega\times S,\mathcal G\otimes\Sigma)$: the identity map into $(\Omega,\mathcal G)$ is measurable because $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$, and $X$ is measurable, so [F9] applies. Therefore $\{g(\omega,X(\omega))\in B\}$ is the measurable preimage of $E$ under this map. Step 2.1 gives measurability and the conditional-event identity for $K_g(\cdot,B)$. For every $\omega$, $K_g(\omega,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of the probability measure $K(\omega,\cdot)$, hence is a probability measure. These are exactly the clauses in [F1], so $K_g$ is a regular conditional distribution of $g(\omega,X(\omega))$.

The tuple $(X,U)$ is measurable into the product space by [F9]. The class of sets in $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal V$ for which the evaluation of $\bar K$ is measurable and the conditional-event identity holds is a lambda-system: complements subtract from the whole-space identity, and disjoint unions follow from countable additivity, measurable increasing limits [F8], and [F6]. It contains all rectangles by step 1.2, so [F2, F7] show that it contains $\Sigma\otimes\mathcal V$. Every section is the product probability measure from [F4]; consequently $\bar K$ is a regular conditional distribution of $(X,U)$ given $\mathcal G$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ be a feature-response measurable
space, let $m\ge0$, and put $n=m+1$. A **split score rule** is a jointly
measurable map $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, where $H$ is a
training statistic with values in the specified measurable rule space
$(\mathcal H,\mathscr H)$. The measurable-statistic convention is that of
[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Once $H=h$ is fixed, calibration and test
scores are $R_i=s(h,Z_i)$; the rule does not change when it scores the
calibration or test example.

A **full score assignment** of length $n$ is a measurable map
$A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n):\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ that is
permutation-equivariant:
$$A(\tau_\pi z)=\tau_\pi A(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z^n\text{ and permutation }\pi.$$
For a candidate response $y$, append $(x,y)$ as the $n$th example and write
$R_i(y)=A_i(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,(x,y))$ and $r=R_n(y)$.

For either a split score vector or a full augmented score vector, the
**nonrandomized upper-rank p-value** of the candidate is
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$
An optional **tie-randomized rank p-value** is defined when a supplied random
variable $U$ has Lebesgue probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of the
data and training information:
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)>r\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)=r\}\bigr)}{m+1}.$$
The added $1$ counts the candidate itself in its tie group. A single such $U$
is shared across a candidate scan. This is an explicit randomization; the
general Markov-kernel definition of a randomized procedure
[[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]] does not assert that arbitrary
kernels have a random-seed representation.

Here “uniform on $[0,1]$” means $\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$.

Smaller scores are treated as more conforming. The rank formula counts all
ties conservatively in the nonrandomized version; the randomized formula
spreads the candidate uniformly over its entire tie block.

derivations.claim: For each $k$-element subset $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let $M_I=\max_{i\in I}R_i$. Then $R_{(k)}=\min_{|I|=k}M_I$: every $k$-element subset has maximum at least the $k$th smallest score, and the subset of the $k$ smallest scores has that maximum exactly. There are finitely many such nonempty subsets, so [F1] makes this finite minimum of finite maxima measurable.
For any two indices, $\{R_i\ge R_j\}=\{R_i-R_j\in[0,+\infty)\}$ is measurable by [F1]–[F3]. The upper-rank p-value is a finite sum of indicators of these events divided by $n$, so is measurable.

On the same domain, the tie count is a finite sum of the comparison indicators from step 1.2. Multiplication by the measurable real function $U$, addition, and division by the positive integer $n$ preserve measurability by [F1]. Hence the randomized rank map is measurable.

List its distinct values in decreasing order $v_1>\cdots>v_s$, let $d_j$ be the multiplicity of $v_j$, and put $D_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^j d_\ell$. Each coordinate in the $j$th tie group has upper rank $D_j/n$. Hence the number of coordinates whose upper rank is at most $u$ is either zero or one of the cumulative counts $D_j\le nu$, and is therefore at most $nu$.

For fixed $r$, the $j$th tie group has $D_{j-1}$ scores strictly above it and $d_j$ scores equal to it, so for any index in that group the randomized rank is $(D_{j-1}+Ud_j)/n$. Averaging uniformly over the $n$ coordinate indices selects this interval with probability $d_j/n$; conditional on the group, its value is uniform on $[D_{j-1}/n,D_j/n]$. These intervals partition $[0,1]$ and their lengths are $d_j/n$, so the averaged rank law is Uniform$[0,1]$.

By exchangeability [F1], each coordinate has the same upper-rank distribution. Thus [F5] and the pointwise bound of step 1.1 give $\mathbb P(p_n\le u)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb P(\frac1n\#\{j:R_j\ge R_i\}\le u)=\mathbb E[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{\frac1n\#\{j:R_j\ge R_i\}\le u\}]\le u$. The last coordinate therefore has a superuniform upper-rank p-value.

Since $R$ is exchangeable and $U$ is independent of $R$ by [F4], permuting score coordinates leaves the joint law of $(R,U)$ unchanged. Thus every randomized coordinate rank has the same distribution, equal to the averaged distribution in step 1.2. In particular $p_{U,n}$ is Uniform$[0,1]$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$, let $X$ be a random element of $(S,\Sigma)$, and let $K$ be a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. If $T$ is a measurable space and $g:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\times(S,\Sigma)\to(T,\Tau)$ is measurable, then
$$K_g(\omega,B):=K\bigl(\omega,\{x:g(\omega,x)\in B\}\bigr),\qquad B\in\Tau,$$
is a regular conditional distribution of $g(\omega,X(\omega))$ given $\mathcal G$.

If, in addition, $U$ is a random element of a measurable space $(V,\mathcal V)$, is independent of $\mathcal G\vee\sigma(X)$, and has law $\lambda$, then $K(\omega,\cdot)\otimes\lambda$ is a regular conditional distribution of $(X,U)$ given $\mathcal G$.

Let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ be an exchangeable random element of $\mathcal Z^n$,
and let $A:\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be measurable and
permutation-equivariant in the sense of
[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]]. Then $A(Z)$ is an
exchangeable real random vector.

Let $R_1,\ldots,R_n$ be an exchangeable real random vector with $n\ge1$.
Define its last-coordinate upper-rank p-value by
$$p_n=\frac1n\#\{i\le n:R_i\ge R_n\}.$$
Then $\mathbb P(p_n\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$. If $U$ has Lebesgue
probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of $R$, define
$$p_{U,n}=\frac{\#\{i\le n:R_i>R_n\}+U\,\#\{i\le n:R_i=R_n\}}n.$$
Then $p_{U,n}$ has the uniform law on $[0,1]$.

Let $m\ge0$ calibration examples $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$ be scored by one fixed,
measurable score rule $s_H$ obtained from the training statistic $H$, and let
$0<\alpha<1$. Set
$$n=m+1,\qquad k=\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil.$$

the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$, so ties are broken by the fixed index order. If
$k\le m$, let $q$ be the score component of the $k$th ordered pair; if
$k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a feature value $x$, return
$$C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s_H(x,y)\le q\}.$$

probability law on $[0,1]$, shared across the candidate scan, and returns
$$C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\},$$

[[def-conformal-nonconformity-score-and-rank-pvalue]]. The candidate score is
included in its tie group. The score maps must be jointly measurable in the
training, calibration, feature, and response variables; then membership in
each returned set is a measurable event by
[[lem-finite-order-statistic-and-rank-maps-are-measurable]].

derivations.claim: Define $g(\omega,z)=(s(H(\omega),z_i))_{i=1}^{m+1}$. For each $i$, the map $(\omega,z)\mapsto(H(\omega),z_i)$ is measurable into $\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z$: the preimage of a rectangle $A\times B$ is $H^{-1}(A)\times\{z:z_i\in B\}$, which belongs to $\mathcal T\otimes\mathscr Z^{\otimes(m+1)}$, and such rectangles generate the target product sigma-algebra. Joint measurability of $s$ therefore makes every coordinate of $g$ measurable. The finite tuple $g$ is measurable into the product Borel sigma-algebra because preimages of Borel rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate preimages. For each fixed $\omega$, $g(\omega,\cdot)$ is permutation-equivariant because the same fixed rule $s(H(\omega),\cdot)$ is applied coordinatewise. By [F2] its pushforward is a regular conditional distribution of the score vector; by the sectionwise exchangeability in the hypothesis and [F3], that score-vector distribution is exchangeable.

Put $n=m+1$ and $k=\lceil n(1-\alpha)\rceil$. If $k=n$, [F5] sets $q=+\infty$, so every true response is covered. If $k\le m$ and the true test score $R_n$ exceeds the $k$th calibration score $q$, then at least $k$ calibration scores are strictly below $R_n$; consequently at most $n-k$ of all $n$ scores are at least $R_n$, and $p_n\le(n-k)/n\le\alpha$. Thus $p_n>\alpha$ implies coverage in every case.

Apply [F4] to the conditional exchangeable score law from step 1.1. The event $p_n>\alpha$ has conditional probability at least $1-\alpha$, and step 1.2 includes it in the nonrandomized coverage event. For the randomized version, the second assertion of [F2] makes $Q_\omega\otimes\lambda$ a regular conditional distribution of $(Z,U)$ given $\mathcal T$. The map that sends $(\omega,z,u)$ to the tie-randomized rank computed from $g(\omega,z)$ and $u$ is jointly measurable: the score coordinates are measurable by step 1.1, comparisons of real-valued measurable functions are measurable, and the rank formula uses finite sums, products, and scalar division. For almost every $\omega$, $Q_\omega$ is exchangeable, $H(\omega)$ is fixed, and $\lambda$ is independent uniform; [F4] therefore gives conditional probability exactly $1-\alpha$ for $p_{U,n}>\alpha$, which is precisely randomized-set coverage.

[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Once $H=h$ is fixed, calibration and test
scores are $R_i=s(h,Z_i)$; the rule does not change when it scores the
calibration or test example.

A **full score assignment** of length $n$ is a measurable map
$A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n):\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ that is
permutation-equivariant:
$$A(\tau_\pi z)=\tau_\pi A(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z^n\text{ and permutation }\pi.$$
For a candidate response $y$, append $(x,y)$ as the $n$th example and write
$R_i(y)=A_i(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,(x,y))$ and $r=R_n(y)$.

**nonrandomized upper-rank p-value** of the candidate is
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$

kernels have a random-seed representation.

Smaller scores are treated as more conforming. The rank formula counts all
ties conservatively in the nonrandomized version; the randomized formula
spreads the candidate uniformly over its entire tie block.
